newsitem.title: FRANCE: EMU success hangs on Franco-German accord on central bank.
newsitem.headline: EMU success hangs on Franco-German accord on central bank.

text.p: The success of the European Union's drive towards monetary union hinges largely on France's ability to respect Germany's deeply-rooted need to guard against inflation through a central bank independent of politicians.
Economists said whether France and Germany can reconcile their very different visions of how to manage the single currency was the fundamental question ahead of monetary union, due inm 1999.
While France wants an actively managed currency, subject to democratic supervision, Germany wants stability, reinforced by a central bank wholly independent of political control.
"There is a clear conflict between France and Germany," Joerg Kraemer, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt said. "There is a different history of thinking about central banks."
"That's clearly going to be the story of the next six months," UBS economist Darren Williams said.

At a summit meeting this weekend, French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl showed the political will was there on both sides to press ahead with Economic and Monetary Union regardless of these differences.
Both appear to have instructed their finance ministers to come up with a compromise deal last Thursday on a post-EMU budget discipline pact even if it took all night.

As a result finance ministers did just that -- in marathon session of talks that finally delivered a stability pact reconciling France's view that politicians must remain firmly in control of fiscal policy with Germany's desire to clip government's wings with the threat of fines if they overspend.
"If there is a conflict which could endanger EMU in 1999, Kohl stands ready to make compromises in order to save the idea," Kraemer said.

Chirac in turn pledged again in a television interview on Thursday night that there would be no change in French policies, and made a point of ruling out any devaluation in the franc against the mark as "unacceptable for the Germans".
But no sooner was the stability pact agreed, than Chirac started marking out the next line in the sand on EMU policy.
There must be, he repeated, a political body to counterbalance the European Central Bank (ECB).
This would be a council made up of ministers and heads of government of the countries in the euro, he said.

French officials said Chirac wanted something similar to the Group of Seven, launched as an informal gathering of rich nations by France, and with no institutional framework nor binding power. It can meet at the level either of finance ministers or heads of states and government.

That balance, economists say, depends on France respecting Germany's need to maintain an independent central bank -- seen as the only reliable guardian against inflation, a near obsession of Germans whose savings were wiped out by the hyper-inflation of 1920s and 30s. The future European central bank's independence is enshrined in the Maastricht treaty.

As long as he stops at that, France's European partners look as though they will go along with the idea, provided it does not divide Europe in two between those inside the euro zone and those left out. French sources say Bonn is in favour.
"It will be sufficient to have an informal G7-like meeting," Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker told Reuters Financial Television.

But any sign that Chirac wants these summits to talk too loudly about exchange rates, or push too aggressively for a rise in the dollar, is likely to undermine the delicate balance found by France and Germany over the stability pact.
But while in Germany, exchange rate policy is very much subordinated to monetary policy, French officials stress that politicians and not technocrats must decide the external value of the euro.
Chirac already laid down a marker of troubles ahead by hinting France might block the appointment of Dutch central banker Wim Duisenberg as head of the ECB.

Duisenberg, seen as a safe pair of hands in the style of Bundesbank-head Hans Tietmeyer, had been assumed to be the obvious candidate after he was named head of the ECB's forerunner, the European Monetary Institute.
